title: What silica training does OSHA require for construction workers?
description: What 29 CFR 1926.1153(i) requires of silica training in construction, how it links to hazard communication, the competent person and the evidence to keep.
shortAnswer: The Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) requires construction employers covered by the respirable crystalline silica standard, 29 CFR 1926.1153, to include silica in their hazard communication program and to ensure each covered employee can demonstrate knowledge and understanding of six topics in paragraph (i)(2), including the health hazards, the tasks that create exposure, the employer's controls, the competent person's identity and medical surveillance. The test is demonstrated understanding, not attendance.
keyTakeaways: The standard covers all occupational exposure to respirable crystalline silica in construction unless exposure will remain below 25 micrograms per cubic meter as an 8-hour time-weighted average under any foreseeable conditions.
Paragraph (i)(1) folds silica into the Hazard Communication Standard (29 CFR 1910.1200) and requires training to address cancer, lung effects, immune system effects and kidney effects.
Paragraph (i)(2) requires each covered employee to be able to demonstrate knowledge of six named topics, and requires a copy of the standard to be readily available at no cost.
Training must name the competent person designated under paragraph (g)(4), who implements the written exposure control plan.
No fixed retraining interval is set in 1926.1153. Hazard communication training is required at initial assignment and whenever a new chemical hazard is introduced.
jurisdiction: United States (federal, with OSHA-approved State Plans)
regulator: Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA), US Department of Labor
appliesTo: Construction employers whose employees are exposed to respirable crystalline silica at or above 25 micrograms per cubic meter (8-hour TWA) under any foreseeable conditions
Employees performing tasks such as cutting, grinding, drilling or crushing concrete, brick, block, stone and similar materials
Competent persons designated to implement the written exposure control plan
Supervisors and trainers responsible for silica hazard communication

sections.heading: Who does the construction silica training requirement apply to?

blocks.text: It applies to every construction employer whose employees could be exposed to respirable crystalline silica at or above 25 micrograms per cubic meter of air (25 µg/m3) as an 8-hour time-weighted average. Paragraph (a) of [29 CFR 1926.1153](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/29/1926.1153) applies the standard to "all occupational exposures to respirable crystalline silica in construction work, except where employee exposure will remain below 25 micrograms per cubic meter of air ... under any foreseeable conditions."

The exemption is narrow. It requires exposure to stay below the action level under any foreseeable conditions, which is hard to show for crews who regularly saw, grind or drill masonry and concrete. Most general contractors, concrete, masonry, demolition and tile trades therefore treat their exposed workforce as covered and train accordingly.

The standard took effect on June 23, 2016, and paragraph (k) says all obligations except laboratory analysis methods commenced on June 23, 2017. OSHA's [construction silica page](https://www.osha.gov/silica-crystalline/construction) gives September 23, 2017 as the date construction employers had to comply with all requirements other than laboratory evaluation, which began June 23, 2018.

blocks.title: Currency and State Plans
blocks.text: This page reflects 29 CFR 1926.1153 and 1910.1200 as at November 2026. OSHA says there are 22 State Plans covering private sector and public workers, and that State Plans must be at least as effective as OSHA. Employers in State Plan states should check whether their state has adopted different or additional silica rules.

sections.heading: What must silica training cover under paragraph (i)(2)?

blocks.text: It must leave each covered employee able to demonstrate knowledge and understanding of six specific topics. Paragraph (i)(2)(i) requires the employer to "ensure that each employee covered by this section can demonstrate knowledge and understanding of at least the following":

items: the health hazards associated with exposure to respirable crystalline silica
specific tasks in the workplace that could result in exposure
specific measures the employer has implemented to protect employees, including engineering controls, work practices and respirators to be used
the identity of the competent person designated under paragraph (g)(4)
the purpose and a description of the medical surveillance program required by paragraph (h)

blocks.text: Paragraph (i)(2)(ii) adds that the employer must make a copy of the section readily available without cost to each covered employee. Items 2, 3 and 5 cannot be delivered by a generic course: they depend on the employer's own task list, its chosen controls and the name of the person it has designated. A purchased online module can cover items 1, 4 and 6, but the site specific items need the employer's input.

sections.heading: How does silica training connect to hazard communication?

blocks.text: Silica training sits inside the employer's hazard communication program, so the HazCom training rules also apply. Paragraph (i)(1) requires the employer to include respirable crystalline silica in its program under the Hazard Communication Standard, ensure access to labels and safety data sheets, train under both the HCS and paragraph (i)(2), and address "at least the following hazards: Cancer, lung effects, immune system effects, and kidney effects."

For construction, [29 CFR 1926.59](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/29/1926.59) says the requirements are identical to [29 CFR 1910.1200](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/29/1910.1200). Paragraph (h)(1) of that standard requires effective information and training "at the time of their initial assignment, and whenever a new chemical hazard the employees have not previously been trained about is introduced into their work area." Paragraph (h)(3) requires training on detection methods, the physical and health hazards, protective measures, and the details of the employer's program, including labels and safety data sheets.

Hazard communication was the second most frequently cited standard in federal OSHA's preliminary list for fiscal year 2026 (October 1, 2025 to August 31, 2026), according to OSHA's [top 10 cited standards](https://www.osha.gov/top10citedstandards) page. The general hazard communication duty is described on the [OSHA training requirements](/regulations/osha-training-requirements) page. This page covers what silica adds to it.

sections.heading: What does the competent person need to know?

blocks.text: The competent person must be able to identify existing and foreseeable silica hazards and have authority to correct them promptly. The standard defines a competent person as someone "capable of identifying existing and foreseeable respirable crystalline silica hazards in the workplace" with "authorization to take prompt corrective measures to eliminate or minimize them," and with "the knowledge and ability necessary to fulfill the responsibilities set forth in paragraph (g)."

Paragraph (g) is the written exposure control plan. It must describe exposure tasks, the controls for each task, housekeeping measures and procedures to restrict access. The plan must be reviewed at least annually, and paragraph (g)(4) requires the employer to designate a competent person "to make frequent and regular inspections of job sites, materials, and equipment to implement the written exposure control plan." The standard does not prescribe a course for this role, so the employer must be able to show how the person's knowledge was established, for example through role specific training and a documented assessment.

The competent person also needs to understand Table 1, the task based list of engineering controls, work practices and respirator requirements that employers can follow instead of measuring exposure. For tasks not on Table 1, or where Table 1 is not fully followed, paragraph (d) applies a permissible exposure limit of 50 µg/m3 as an 8-hour TWA and requires an exposure assessment.

sections.heading: How often is silica training required, and what records are needed?

blocks.text: 1926.1153 sets no annual refresher; training is tied to assignment and to change. Because the duty is that each employee "can demonstrate" knowledge, the employer must retrain whenever that is no longer true: when tasks, controls or the competent person change, or when observation shows a worker cannot explain the controls they are using. Hazard communication adds a trigger whenever a new chemical hazard is introduced.

The standard's recordkeeping paragraph (j) covers air monitoring data, objective data and medical surveillance, not training. Training records are therefore not expressly required by 1926.1153, but without them an employer has little way to prove that employees can demonstrate the required knowledge. Medical surveillance is required for each employee who must use a respirator for 30 or more days per year, which is also the group that most needs item 6 explained. For record design, see [how long to keep training records](/guides/how-long-to-keep-training-records).

sections.heading: How can an employer map silica duties to training and evidence?

blocks.text: Map each paragraph (i) topic to the person responsible, the trigger, and a piece of evidence that shows understanding, not just attendance. The table below is an original, illustrative mapping for a construction employer. It is a starting point for a [training matrix](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix), not a compliance template.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry structures the silica standard as a framework of tasks, controls, roles and required knowledge before any course is written, then links each paragraph (i)(2) topic to an assessment point. When a site adds a task or changes a control, the affected roles and assessments are identified from the framework instead of by rereading every course.

faqs.q: Does a worker who only occasionally cuts concrete need silica training?
faqs.a: If that worker's exposure could reach 25 µg/m3 as an 8-hour TWA under any foreseeable conditions, the standard applies and paragraph (i) training is required. The exemption depends on exposure, not on how often the task is done. Employers relying on the exemption should be able to show why exposure stays below the action level.

faqs.q: Is a generic online silica course enough?
faqs.a: Not on its own. A generic course can explain health effects, the standard and medical surveillance, but paragraph (i)(2) also requires workers to know the specific tasks on their site, the employer's specific controls and respirators, and the name of the designated competent person. Those topics need site specific delivery and evidence.

faqs.q: Is silica training required every year?
faqs.a: 1926.1153 does not set an annual interval. Training is required so that each covered employee can demonstrate knowledge, and hazard communication training is required at initial assignment and when new hazards are introduced. Many employers choose a periodic refresher, but that is a policy choice, not a rule in the standard.

faqs.q: Does the general industry silica standard have the same training rules?
faqs.a: General industry and maritime are covered by a separate standard, 29 CFR 1910.1053, which this page does not cover. Construction employers should work from 1926.1153, which includes Table 1 task controls and the competent person requirement that apply to construction.
